In the midst of iPhone launch week madness, one of my favorite brands has unveiled their brand-new retro-styled dock for the Mac mini and Mac Studio. Last year, they released the Retro Dock for the M4 Mac mini—a perfect combination of functionality, form, and nostalgia I've never seen before. It added tons of ports, an NVMe storage slot, and a 5-inch display, all wrapped in a shell that looks like the original 1984 Macintosh. The new Wokyis G5 and G7 take this design to another level. They add more professional-grade ports, a larger display, useful physical buttons, while retaining that retro look and feel, and expand compatibility to both the Mac mini and Mac Studio. Here's what you need to know.

Be sure to check out my unboxing and review video, which truly shows how I'm integrating the G7 into my workflow.

I highly recommend watching the unboxing video above to get a true sense of how cool and unique this dock's design is. But beyond the look and nostalgia, you're also getting a powerful 16-in-1 dock featuring a 7-inch display, high-speed connectivity, professional-grade ports, physical control keys, and NVMe SSD enclosure. Wokyis offers the G5 (Mac mini) and G7 (Mac Studio) in both 10 Gbps and 80 Gbps configurations. I tested the G7 for Mac Studio. Here are some key specs you need to know:

  • 7-inch tiltable IPS 1280×800 display
  • Nine physical customizable shortcut keys
  • 80Gbps model features Thunderbolt 5 connectivity
  • M.2 NVMe SSD enclosure supporting up to 8TB
  • CFexpress Type B card reader with speeds up to 1,000MB/s
  • SD and Micro SD 4.0 card readers with speeds up to 312MB/s
  • 2 USB-C ports with speeds up to 10Gbps
  • 2 USB-A ports with speeds up to 10Gbps
  • 2 additional USB A 2.0 ports
  • DisplayPort output supporting up to 8K 60Hz
  • HDMI port
  • 3.5mm headphone jack

Everything you need comes in the box, including the dock itself, a screwdriver for installing the NVMe enclosure, a thermal pad for the SSD, and two 10Gbps braided USB-C cables. It's worth noting that while it's designed to physically mount on top of a Mac mini or Mac Studio, you can also use it as a standalone dock with any USB-C computer.

Thunderbolt 5 is another major feature of the 80 Gbps flagship model. When you connect the dock to your Mac, the 80 Gbps connection allows supported NVMe SSDs to achieve speeds close to internal storage. So you no longer need to pay Apple's premium to upgrade your internal storage. Even with SSD storage prices at record highs, buying an NVMe SSD is still cheaper than upgrading your computer's internal storage.

But in actual use, how do these features perform?

My experience with the G7

The first thing that drew me to buy this dock was its design. The Mac Studio is an incredibly powerful and efficient computer, but its minimalist design makes it look like a large, cold silver box, lacking personality. Placing the G7 on top completely transforms the Mac's look and feel. This time, Wokyis has decided to win the hearts of retro gaming enthusiasts. The ivory white color scheme, D-pad, red action buttons, and tiltable display instantly add a nostalgic gaming aesthetic to the whole setup. Of course, this look is an instant conversation starter for anyone who walks into my office. But once you've seen enough of the look, you'll discover it actually adds surprisingly practical features.

The physical buttons on the body actually have real functions—they handle volume adjustment, media playback, copy, paste, screenshots, screen brightness, and display controls. Speaking of the display, I initially thought it was just a gimmick, but it's surprisingly useful. macOS recognizes it as a regular external monitor, so any window or app can be moved over, and it scales perfectly in real time. It's a 7-inch IPS panel with 1280×800 resolution. I mainly use it for passively viewing information and content. You usually see me with a video podcast playing while handling administrative work, but when using Final Cut Pro, I use it as a color monitoring system. It performs exceptionally well for this purpose. But the uses are endless: you can use it as a clock, view messages, display widgets, monitor your system, and reportedly Wokyis is also working on an official utility app optimized for this display.

But for me, the biggest practical benefit is storage expansion. I use a 4TB NVMe SSD to store all my important files and documents, run all my FCP projects, and even install apps on it, ensuring the internal storage doesn't get too full. Combined with the rich port selection, I personally don't use CF Express cards in my workflow, but having this slot is very useful for others' workflows. My most-used ports are the microSD card slot and the 10Gbps USB-C ports. The G7 essentially replaced several accessories that would otherwise be scattered across my desk.

The G5 version for Mac mini offers roughly the same features, just smaller, with a 5-inch display instead of 7 inches. The G7 version is compatible with any Mac Studio, while the G5 works with the M4 Mac mini or newer. As I mentioned earlier, both versions can also be used with any computer that has USB-C connectivity.

Pricing and availability

Wokyis G5 and G7 are available for pre-order on Kickstarter starting today, with global shipping expected to begin in October 2026. Pricing for each model is as follows:

  • Wokyis G5 for Mac mini (10Gbps) — $99
  • Wokyis G5 for Mac mini (80Gbps) — $199
  • Wokyis G7 for Mac Studio (10Gbps) — $109
  • Wokyis G5 for Mac mini (80Gbps) — $219

If you want additional accessories, they offer other bundle combinations. If you're in the market for a new USB-C hub, the early bird pricing is an absolute steal. The final retail price for the Wokyis G7 80Gbps version will be $369.

Final verdict

For me, this product's selling points are uniqueness and functionality. Tech products are looking increasingly cold and impersonal because they've become tools and equipment. These Macs now run so smoothly thanks to excellent software-hardware integration that the hardware itself doesn't need to be fancy. This space is perfect for products like the Wokyis G5 and G7, which add personality and nostalgia, instantly becoming a conversation piece in any environment. But the key point is it's not just a pretty shell—it has real functionality. The display is genuinely very practical and useful. It's equipped with all the professional-grade ports you need, and can also help expand your storage.

So if you're looking for a new Mac hub, or you know a tech enthusiast who would definitely love this product, I think considering the price, performance, and nostalgia factor, this product is absolutely worth recommending.

What do you think? Would you use a product like this? Share your thoughts in the comments!
